text: Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in. I drink at it; but while I drink I see the sandy bottom and detect how shallow it is. Its thin current slides away, but eternity remains.
author: Henry David Thoreau
locator: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For

text: We must learn to reawaken and keep ourselves awake, not by mechanical aids, but by an infinite expectation of the dawn, which does not forsake us in our soundest sleep. I know of no more encouraging fact than the unquestionable ability of man to elevate his life by a conscious endeavor.
author: Henry David Thoreau
locator: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For

text: There were times when I could not afford to sacrifice the bloom of the present moment to any work, whether of the head or hands. I love a broad margin to my life.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: I find it wholesome to be alone the greater part of the time. To be in company, even with the best, is soon wearisome and dissipating. I love to be alone. I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: I had three chairs in my house; one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: I learned this, at least, by my experiment; that if one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams, and endeavors to live the life which he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: If you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost; that is where they should be. Now put the foundations under them.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Why should we be in such desperate haste to succeed, and in such desperate enterprises? If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer. Let him step to the music which he hears, however measured or far away.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: However mean your life is, meet it and live it; do not shun it and call it hard names. It is not so bad as you are. It looks poorest when you are richest. The fault-finder will find faults even in paradise.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: It is easy in the world to live after the world’s opinion; it is easy in solitude to live after our own; but the great man is he who in the midst of the crowd keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Nothing can bring you peace but yourself. Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: There is a time in every man’s education when he arrives at the conviction that envy is ignorance; that imitation is suicide; that he must take himself for better for worse as his portion; that though the wide universe is full of good, no kernel of nourishing corn can come to him but through his toil bestowed on that plot of ground which is given to him to till.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: These roses under my window make no reference to former roses or to better ones; they are for what they are; they exist with God to-day. There is no time to them. There is simply the rose; it is perfect in every moment of its existence.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: A friend is a person with whom I may be sincere. Before him I may think aloud.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm. The way of life is wonderful; it is by abandonment.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: To finish the moment, to find the journey's end in every step of the road, to live the greatest number of good hours, is wisdom.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Life is a series of surprises, and would not be worth taking or keeping if it were not.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Rings and other jewels are not gifts, but apologies for gifts. The only gift is a portion of thyself.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: These enchantments are medicinal, they sober and heal us. These are plain pleasures, kindly and native to us.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: When I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep. Nay, when I walk alone in a beautiful orchard, if my thoughts are some part of the time taken up with external occurrences, I some part of the time call them back again to my walk, to the orchard, to the sweetness of that solitude, and to myself.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: He who fears he shall suffer, already suffers what he fears.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Wherever your life ends, it is all there. The utility of living consists not in the length of days, but in the use of time; a man may have lived long, and yet lived but a little. Make use of time while it is present with you.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, ch. 19, That to Study Philosophy Is to Learn to Die

text: I would always have a man to be doing, and, as much as in him lies, to extend and spin out the offices of life; and then let death take me planting my cabbages, indifferent to him, and still less of my gardens not being finished.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, ch. 19, That to Study Philosophy Is to Learn to Die

text: The most manifest sign of wisdom is a continual cheerfulness; her state is like that of things in the regions above the moon, always clear and serene.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, ch. 25, Of the Education of Children

text: The greatest thing in the world is for a man to know that he is his own.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: No one lays down a certain design for his life, and we only deliberate thereof by pieces.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book II, ch. 1, Of the Inconstancy of Our Actions

text: Hatred is increased by being reciprocated, and can on the other hand be destroyed by love.
author: Benedict de Spinoza

text: A free man thinks of death least of all things; and his wisdom is a meditation not of death but of life.
author: Benedict de Spinoza

text: Blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself; neither do we rejoice therein, because we control our lusts, but, contrariwise, because we rejoice therein, we are able to control our lusts.
author: Benedict de Spinoza

text: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
author: Benedict de Spinoza

text: For what a man is in himself, what accompanies him when he is alone, what no one can give or take away, is obviously more essential to him than everything he has in the way of possessions, or even what he may be in the eyes of the world.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
locator: Chapter I, Division of the Subject

text: Each day is a little life: every waking and rising a little birth, every fresh morning a little youth, every going to rest and sleep a little death.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer

text: The present alone is true and actual; it is the only time which possesses full reality, and our existence lies in it exclusively. Therefore we should always be glad of it, and give it the welcome it deserves, and enjoy every hour that is bearable by its freedom from pain and annoyance with a full consciousness of its value.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer

text: How can a man come to know himself? Never by thinking, but by doing. Try to do your duty, and you will know at once what you are worth.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Everything that frees our spirit without giving us control of ourselves is ruinous.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are two powers that make for peace: what is right, and what is fitting.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: He is the happiest man who can set the end of his life in connection with the beginning.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A rainbow which lasts a quarter of an hour is looked at no more.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is a politeness of the heart, and it is allied to love. It produces the most agreeable politeness of outward demeanour.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is not enough to know, we must also apply; it is not enough to will, we must also do.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Every man hears only what he understands.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Wherefore, O judges, be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty, that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
author: Plato

text: Love all God’s creation, the whole and every grain of sand in it. Love every leaf, every ray of God’s light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will perceive the divine mystery in things.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: You must know that there is nothing higher and stronger and more wholesome and good for life in the future than some good memory, especially a memory of childhood, of home. People talk to you a great deal about your education, but some good, sacred memory, preserved from childhood, is perhaps the best education.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text:
I celebrate myself, and sing myself,
And what I assume you shall assume,
For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you.
author: Walt Whitman

text:
I loafe and invite my soul,
I lean and loafe at my ease observing a spear of summer grass.
author: Walt Whitman

text:
I exist as I am, that is enough,
If no other in the world be aware I sit content,
And if each and all be aware I sit content.
author: Walt Whitman

text:
Do I contradict myself?
Very well then I contradict myself,
(I am large, I contain multitudes.)
author: Walt Whitman

text:
I bequeath myself to the dirt to grow from the grass I love,
If you want me again look for me under your boot-soles.
author: Walt Whitman

text:
Failing to fetch me at first keep encouraged,
Missing me one place search another,
I stop somewhere waiting for you.
author: Walt Whitman

text:
Afoot and light-hearted I take to the open road,
Healthy, free, the world before me,
The long brown path before me leading wherever I choose.
author: Walt Whitman

text: The morning sea of silence broke into ripples of bird songs; and the flowers were all merry by the roadside; and the wealth of gold was scattered through the rift of the clouds while we busily went on our way and paid no heed.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Light, my light, the world-filling light, the eye-kissing light, heart-sweetening light! Ah, the light dances, my darling, at the centre of my life; the light strikes, my darling, the chords of my love; the sky opens, the wind runs wild, laughter passes over the earth.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: On the seashore of endless worlds children meet. The infinite sky is motionless overhead and the restless water is boisterous. On the seashore of endless worlds the children meet with shouts and dances.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: The same stream of life that runs through my veins night and day runs through the world and dances in rhythmic measures. It is the same life that shoots in joy through the dust of the earth in numberless blades of grass and breaks into tumultuous waves of leaves and flowers.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Deliverance is not for me in renunciation. I feel the embrace of freedom in a thousand bonds of delight.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: When I go from hence let this be my parting word, that what I have seen is unsurpassable.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: If you shed tears when you miss the sun, you also miss the stars.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: I sit at my window this morning where the world like a passer-by stops for a moment, nods to me and goes.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Rest belongs to the work as the eyelids to the eyes.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: We read the world wrong and say that it deceives us.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Let life be beautiful like summer flowers and death like autumn leaves.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: He who wants to do good knocks at the gate; he who loves finds the gate open.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Be still, my heart, these great trees are prayers.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: The roots below the earth claim no rewards for making the branches fruitful.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: The water in a vessel is sparkling; the water in the sea is dark. The small truth has words that are clear; the great truth has great silence.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life’s longing for itself.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: You give but little when you give of your possessions. It is when you give of yourself that you truly give.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: When you work you are a flute through whose heart the whispering of the hours turns to music.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: Your joy is your sorrow unmasked. And the selfsame well from which your laughter rises was oftentimes filled with your tears.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: The teacher who walks in the shadow of the temple, among his followers, gives not of his wisdom but rather of his faith and his lovingness. If he is indeed wise he does not bid you enter the house of his wisdom, but rather leads you to the threshold of your own mind.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: Your friend is your needs answered. He is your field which you sow with love and reap with thanksgiving. And he is your board and your fireside.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text:
If I can stop one heart from breaking,
I shall not live in vain;
If I can ease one life the aching,
Or cool one pain,
Or help one fainting robin
Unto his nest again,
I shall not live in vain.
author: Emily Dickinson

text:
Hope is the thing with feathers
That perches in the soul,
And sings the tune without the words,
And never stops at all,
And sweetest in the gale is heard;
And sore must be the storm
That could abash the little bird
That kept so many warm.
author: Emily Dickinson

text:
A word is dead
When it is said,
Some say.
I say it just
Begins to live
That day.
author: Emily Dickinson

text:
There is no frigate like a book
To take us lands away,
Nor any coursers like a page
Of prancing poetry.
This traverse may the poorest take
Without oppress of toll;
How frugal is the chariot
That bears a human soul!
author: Emily Dickinson

text:
The brain is wider than the sky,
For, put them side by side,
The one the other will include
With ease, and you beside.
author: Emily Dickinson

text:
O servant, where dost thou seek Me?
Lo! I am beside thee.
author: Kabir
Kabir

text: The moon shines in my body, but my blind eyes cannot see it: The moon is within me, and so is the sun. The unstruck drum of Eternity is sounded within me; but my deaf ears cannot hear it.
author: Kabir

text: The river and its waves are one surf: where is the difference between the river and its waves? When the wave rises, it is the water; and when it falls, it is the same water again.
author: Kabir

text: O my heart! the Supreme Spirit, the great Master, is near you: wake, oh wake! Run to the feet of your Beloved: for your Lord stands near to your head. You have slept for unnumbered ages; this morning will you not wake?
author: Kabir

text: Be strong, and enter into your own body: for there your foothold is firm.
author: Kabir

text: The strains of love fill the days and the nights with music, and the world is listening to its melodies: Mad with joy, life and death dance to the rhythm of this music. The hills and the sea and the earth dance. The world of man dances in laughter and tears.
author: Kabir

text: I laugh when I hear that the fish in the water is thirsty: You do not see that the Real is in your home, and you wander from forest to forest listlessly!
author: Kabir

text: The flute of the Infinite is played without ceasing, and its sound is love: When love renounces all limits, it reaches truth.
author: Kabir

text: I hear the melody of His flute, and I cannot contain myself: The flower blooms, though it is not spring; and already the bee has received its invitation.
author: Kabir

text: Ask not, who hath said this or that, but look to what he says.
author: Thomas à Kempis

text: Who hath a harder battle to fight than he who striveth for self-mastery?
author: Thomas à Kempis

text: First keep thyself in peace, and then shalt thou be able to be a peacemaker towards others. A peaceable man doth more good than a well-learned.
author: Thomas à Kempis
